nodes.text: Neural retrieval models are usually trained and tested on the same dataset, so their behaviour on other domains and tasks is unknown.
nodes.audience_note: reader must know what retrieval and zero-shot mean

nodes.text: Training data are costly, so many retrieval systems are deployed zero-shot.
Lexical methods (BM25) dominate retrieval history; neural sparse, dense, late-interaction and re-ranking families each try to close the lexical gap.
Earlier benchmarks (MultiReQA, KILT) cover one task or one domain, small corpora or Wikipedia.
Among the benchmarks the paper cites, none evaluates retrieval zero-shot across many tasks and domains with large corpora.
RQ1: does in-domain performance predict zero-shot performance?
RQ2: which architectures hold up across heterogeneous datasets, and at what computational cost?
RQ3: does existing relevance annotation treat non-lexical systems fairly?
Build a heterogeneous zero-shot benchmark and use it to compare ten systems from five families.
BEIR: 18 English datasets, 9 tasks, unified format and software; nDCG@10; MS MARCO-trained checkpoints evaluated without adaptation.
Zero-shot evaluation of ten systems on 18 datasets with nDCG@10, plus MS MARCO in-domain scores.
Latency and index-size measurement on 1M DBPedia documents.
Manually judge the unjudged top-10 hits ('holes') of every system on TREC-COVID and re-score.
Train two identical models differing only in similarity function to test the document-length preference.
Zero-shot scores: BM25 strong; BM25+CE and ColBERT best on average; docT5query above BM25 on 11 of 18; dense and sparse-learned often below BM25; GenQ helps specialised domains.
Best zero-shot systems are the slowest; ColBERT needs the largest index.
Hole@10 differs widely by system; adding judgements barely changes lexical systems but lifts ANCE and ColBERT.
Cosine versus dot product changes TREC-COVID nDCG@10 by 15.3 points and the length of retrieved documents.
In-domain scores do not order systems as zero-shot scores do; cross-attention style scoring and keyword expansion are the authors' candidate explanations.
Accuracy of the best systems is bought with latency and index size.
Pools built by lexical systems disadvantage non-lexical systems, at least on TREC-COVID.
The similarity function is the authors' explanation for TAS-B's preference for short documents.

A heterogeneous zero-shot retrieval benchmark with software, a ten-system comparison in which no system wins everywhere and BM25 remains strong, and evidence of annotation bias against non-lexical systems.
Benchmark scope: English only, short documents, text only, one or two fields, general-purpose models, datasets used as released.
No variance across runs and no total compute reported.
TREC-COVID pool still favours lexical systems; unbiased datasets are needed.
Writer-derived caveats: one-dataset annotation study, single hardware, confounded systems, average row, count discrepancy, few queries, re-implementations, author-made judgements.
Retrieval methods should be evaluated across many datasets; datasets need diverse pooling.
Multilingual, long-document, multi-factor, multi-field and task-specific evaluation.
nDCG@10, qrels, pooling and holes, bi-encoder versus cross-encoder versus late interaction, lexical gap.

experiment_chains.experiment: Zero-shot comparison of ten systems on 18 datasets
experiment_chains.hypothesis: If in-domain scores predicted zero-shot scores, MS MARCO ordering would match BEIR ordering; a mismatch counts against it.
experiment_chains.next: Cost: the best systems are slower, so what do latency and index size look like?

experiment_chains.experiment: Latency and index size on 1M DBPedia documents
experiment_chains.hypothesis: Systems that score best zero-shot pay in latency and index size.
experiment_chains.falsifier: best systems are also fast and small
experiment_chains.design_rationale: efficiency matters for real-time use (authors' framing: models compare a query against millions of documents)
experiment_chains.next: Why do some dense systems fall below BM25 (TREC-COVID)? Look at labels and at document length.

experiment_chains.falsifier: scores of dense systems unchanged after annotation
experiment_chains.next: A second cause of dense-model differences: retrieved document length.

experiment_chains.hypothesis: The similarity function determines whether short or long documents are retrieved.
experiment_chains.falsifier: same length distribution under both similarity functions
experiment_chains.next: Wrap up: what the benchmark shows and what it cannot.
